captions.linkedin:
The riskiest-looking stocks in the market earn the lowest returns. CAPM says the opposite. 📊

Dichev (1998, JF) found it first. Campbell, Hilscher and Szilagyi (2008, JF) reconfirmed it with a hazard model. Firms with the highest bankruptcy risk produce negative alphas, not a fat risk premium.

The distress anomaly is what happens when retail buys lottery odds, institutions can't short the names (borrow is impossible), and the mispricing just sits there.

Here's the complete logic. No black box:

🔹 OHLSON LOGIT, compute the 9-term O-score per firm.
🔹 DECILE BUCKETS, rank firms by O-score every fiscal year.
🔹 INVERSE RISK, long the healthy decile, short the distressed.
🔹 ANNUAL FORMATION, rebalance on fresh accounting data.
🔹 DELISTING TRACK, include full bankruptcy and delisting returns or you'll fool yourself.

Long-only variant: own healthy, skip distressed. Most of the spread survives.

Why traders miss this: the names look cheap. Low P/B, low P/E, beaten down. Classic value screens load on them. An O-score overlay strips out the worst slice without giving up the cheap end.
